title: The Fool: Beginning Before You Know

quickTake.upright: A fresh start worth trying. Look where you are stepping first.
quickTake.reversed: You may be rushing ahead, or never quite daring to begin.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: A fresh start worth trying. Look where you are stepping first.

Reversed in a sentence: You may be rushing ahead, or never quite daring to begin.

The most revealing thing about the Fool is that his face and feet point to different concerns: his face turns toward the distance, while his feet have already reached the cliff edge. Expectation and risk share this moment.

sections.title: Looking into the Distance, Standing at the Edge
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Yellow sky fills most of the picture, with a white sun appearing at the upper right. A young man wears a patterned tunic and a hat with a red feather. He looks upward toward the left of the picture. His right hand holds a long black staff across his shoulder, with a small bundle hanging behind it; his left hand lightly supports a white rose. His luggage is modest, and his posture relaxed and open.

Look lower down: one foot is close to the rocky edge, while the other is lifted behind him. A small white dog leaps at his feet, and blue-and-white mountains stand in the distance. The picture does show a cliff, but it shows neither a fall nor where his next step will land. Whether the dog is accompanying him, warning him, or following excitedly has no single answer in the image itself.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_00_Fool.jpg)

Now connect three details: the bundle shows that the traveler has not brought nothing; the rose leaves something delicate in his hand; the cliff means imagination alone cannot determine the next step. In a modern reading, these can prompt three questions: What experience can I take with me? What curiosity do I want to retain? Which risk must I check first? The white dog need not always mean a “benefactor” or an “obstacle.” A real-world warning may be incomplete and still deserve a hearing. If a redrawn deck puts a bridge or railing beneath the figure, the composition of risk has changed. Look again at the footing rather than reciting the cliff interpretation.

sections.title: Waite's Traveler in Search of Experience
sections.bodyMarkdown:
In his account of the card's symbolism, Waite describes the figure as a spiritual traveler seeking experience. He specifically notes that the figure is paused at this pictured moment, yet retains the eagerness of walking. This gives the Fool momentum while leaving room to choose the next step.

The familiar modern phrase “a new beginning” is a useful learning theme to develop from this picture. It should not be treated as a literal translation of all Waite's old divinatory entries. His separate entry for the Fool differs considerably from this description of a spiritual traveler.

sections.title: Trying Pottery for the First Time
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xiaohe asks, “I want to learn pottery. How can I start in a way that makes me less likely to give up halfway?”

Known facts: She has saved many pictures of pottery but has never handled clay. Nearby options include single introductory sessions and a six-month course requiring full payment in advance. She has only one free evening each week. She draws the upright Fool in the advice position.

The Fool's upturned face and cliff edge correspond to her attraction to finished pieces and her unfamiliarity with the actual cost of practicing. The little bundle can become a limited investment: this time, learn how clay feels and how classes fit her schedule, rather than rushing into a long-term identity as a pottery enthusiast. The reading cannot promise that she is talented or interpret one failure as proof she is unsuited to it. What the first class really needs to answer is whether she wants to keep kneading clay, cleaning up, and waiting for firing.

Another possibility: If she has actually practiced for six months and is only worried about being judged when she enrolls, “try it first” would underestimate her preparation. The question should instead be what kind of feedback would support further learning. If the cost already exceeds what she can afford, look for a free open day first.

A practical next step: Attend one affordable introductory session. Afterwards, separately note the parts of the process she liked and disliked, then check transport, material costs, and cancellation terms. Wait until she has practiced twice before deciding on a long-term arrangement, bringing her interest out of photographs and into a real week.

sections.title: A New Friend: Let Enthusiasm Keep Pace with Understanding
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Ayuan asks, “A friend I've just met has invited me on a trip. Should I agree now?”

Known facts: They have met only once and got along very well. The trip has no clear accommodation arrangements, and the other person wants full payment that day. Ayuan does not want to spoil the mood. He draws the reversed Fool in the position indicating what needs attention.

The reading chosen here is “moving faster than your understanding,” because payment and accommodation information really is missing, not because the new friend must be unreliable. The cliff edge brings attention back to footing: liking someone can be genuine while the scope of a commitment already exceeds the experience they have shared. Reversal invites him to check whether he has confused “staying open” with “not being allowed to ask questions.”

Another possibility: If the itinerary is transparent, refund terms are clear, and the two already have dependable shared experiences, the reversed card might point to excessive fear of a new relationship. In that case, they could discuss a smaller shared activity rather than rejecting every invitation.

A practical next step: Ask the other person to complete the arrangements, hold off on paying an amount he could not afford to lose, and suggest a short daytime outing. The way the person responds to reasonable questions becomes new real-world information. The card itself is not responsible for judging their character.

sections.title: A Small Exercise
sections.bodyMarkdown: Write down one small thing you have long wanted to try. Add two lines: “The cost of experimenting that I am willing to accept is…” and “I will reassess after….” Make the first step small enough to complete this week.

title: The Magician: Putting the Tools at Hand to Work

quickTake.upright: You have skills and resources. You can get something moving.
quickTake.reversed: Plenty of ideas, little follow-through, or effort aimed in the wrong direction.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: You have skills and resources. You can get something moving.

Reversed in a sentence: Plenty of ideas, little follow-through, or effort aimed in the wrong direction.

The Magician's table is already set. Before looking for mysterious powers in this card, notice what is already on the table and how the person behind it intends to use it.

sections.title: One Hand Up, One Hand Down
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Against a bright yellow background, a figure in a white inner robe and red outer garment faces the viewer. His right hand, on the left of the picture, holds aloft a short white wand tapered at both ends. His left hand reaches down, its index finger pointing toward the ground. A horizontal figure eight floats above his head, and a snake-shaped belt circles his waist.

A cup, sword, pentacle, and horizontally placed wand are recognizable on the table. Red roses hang above; red roses, white lilies, and green leaves intertwine in the foreground. The eye can travel from the raised hand through the figure and tabletop to the garden below: the composition links an intention above, tools at hand, and growth at ground level. That last connection is our reading of the composition.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_01_Magician.jpg)

The four kinds of implements differ, yet one person faces them all. This deserves more attention than simply “having lots of tools”: resources become capability through selection and arrangement. The raised and pointing hands create a sense of direction, while the garden carries the eye to something that grows and needs maintenance. From this, the article proposes a check: Has your plan moved from an idea to something another person can understand? Flowers can inspire a metaphor of cultivation, but they do not prove that wishes automatically attract results. Nor can the snake-shaped belt substitute for practical skills. In a redrawn card with a figure but no table, first ask again where its resources are.

sections.title: From an Occult Gesture to Present-Day Action
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite explains the upward and downward gesture as the transmission of grace, power, and light from above to below, and associates the four suit implements with elements of natural life. He also connects the garden flowers with cultivating aspiration. These ideas have a distinct religious and occult background; they do not guarantee the modern claim that wanting something is enough to make it happen.

Drawing on that background, this article reads the Magician as a practical question: How can an inner intention take outward action? Resources include more than objects. They may be skills, time, language, and people you can consult.

[Read Waite's original English text for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar01.htm)

sections.title: Testing an Idea with a Piece of Audio
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xiaoxia asks, “I want to make a neighborhood audio program. Where should I start with the first episode?”

Known facts: She knows how to edit audio and has a phone and headphones. Two shopkeepers she knows are willing to talk about their working days. But she keeps comparing professional recording equipment and has not recorded a single minute. She draws the upright Magician in the available-resources position.

The implements on the table can correspond to skills, equipment, and contacts already available. The hand pointing at the ground turns “I want to make a program” into a playable clip. Since a test recording has not yet revealed what is missing, further shopping does not prove she is better prepared. Upright here is a reminder that resources can be organized, not a prediction that the program will be popular. Interviewees still need to understand how their contributions will be used and agree to participate.

Another possibility: If a test recording reveals that background noise makes the conversation unintelligible, equipment may become a real constraint. She should then test a quieter location or borrow a microphone, rather than ignore feedback to insist that “the tools you already have are enough.”

A practical next step: Get consent first, record a five-minute conversation, edit a one-minute sample, and ask one listener to explain what it was about. Decide what tool to add next only from problems with listening and comprehension. Do not count purchasing as creative progress.

sections.title: Plenty of Promises, Not Enough Concrete Communication
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Linna asks, “We agreed to set aside time together every week. Why do we never manage it?”

Known facts: She and her partner both say they want this, but their dates never have a specific time. She always says, “You decide,” then often declines last-minute invitations because she already has plans. She draws the reversed Magician in the position for what she can adjust herself.

The focus here is the break between words and action. The Magician's tools are on the table, like the couple's existing goodwill and available calendars, but have not been organized into an actionable request. Reversal does not prove anyone is lying or require Linna to take all responsibility for maintaining the relationship. It simply returns to her hands the times, preferences, and limits she can express.

Another possibility: If she has repeatedly suggested workable times and the other person still does not respond, the focus needs to shift from “be more specific” to checking whether their willingness and investment are comparable. The other person's explicit feedback is needed; a card cannot answer for them.

A practical next step: Offer two times she can genuinely attend, explain what she would like to do together, and invite her partner to choose or suggest an option. Try this for two weeks and see whether it happens. If it still falls through, discuss the gap between arrangements and expectations instead of repeating undated promises.

sections.bodyMarkdown: Make three columns: “What I already have,” “What I genuinely lack,” and “What I can finish today.” Once the first two are clear, choose just one action from the third and give it a visible condition for completion.

**Original fictional case.** Xiaoning asks, “How should I handle contradictions in this community oral-history account?”

title: The Empress: Preparing the Conditions for Growth

quickTake.upright: Things grow when they have space and care.
quickTake.reversed: Care is out of balance: perhaps you give too much, or leave yourself out.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Things grow when they have space and care.

Reversed in a sentence: Care is out of balance: perhaps you give too much, or leave yourself out.

The Empress is not busy harvesting in the field. She sits on soft cushions, while the surrounding water, plants, and grain remind us that growth needs an environment, not just urging.

sections.title: The Water, Grain, and Seat Around Her
sections.bodyMarkdown:
She wears a pale gown printed with pomegranates and sits before a red cushion. A crown of stars and green leaves adorns her head. Her right hand raises a scepter topped with a globe, while the other rests naturally beside her lap. Like the soft folds of her clothing, the space around her seat is free of enclosing high walls.

Ripe golden grain fills the foreground, with dense woodland behind. On the right of the picture, a blue stream winds out of the trees and drops into a small waterfall. At the lower left rests a heart-shaped shield bearing the symbol of Venus. Follow the water toward the grain, then back to the human body: this card's abundance is tangible, available to touch, and in need of maintenance.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_03_Empress.jpg)

The card contains many things that have grown, and a person who is sitting down. Seen together, abundance becomes more than a reward for busyness: water, land, and a place to pause make repeated care possible. The scepter remains in the Empress's hand, reminding us that softness does not mean making no choices. A modern application might ask which forms of support you must arrange yourself and which you can accept from others. The grain shows maturity but does not tell us how long growth took. A ripe field cannot tell you how many days a project will take, nor can the Venus shield prove an outcome in love or fertility.

sections.title: Understanding Images of Fruitfulness
sections.bodyMarkdown:

The Venus symbol is a visible historical element of this image; this article does not use it to derive zodiac compatibility or astrological conclusions.

For contemporary learning, “fruitfulness” can extend to creative work, relationships, living conditions, and ongoing care. This extension does not require the reader to have a particular gender, family role, or experience of childbearing.

[Read Waite's original English text for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar03.htm)

sections.title: Understanding the Upright Card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright can ask: What sustainable support does this need in order to grow? Perhaps regular time, sufficient materials, an atmosphere that allows mistakes, or patience that returns only after rest. The Empress's creativity is grounded in the body and daily life.

She also allows you to receive the good things you already have. Eating a proper meal, appreciating your work, or accepting reasonable help need not wait until every task is finished. Being able to feel nourished makes it easier to recognize what deserves continued investment.

sections.title: Understanding the Reversed Card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This article understands reversal as an imbalance in how nourishment is provided. You may keep arranging things for others without asking what they need. Or you may preserve comfort by avoiding the practice new growth requires. Too much care and too little can both limit growth.

Check whether giving is voluntary and sustainable, and whether the recipient still has room for independent choice. If your creative work has stalled, look first for specific conditions rather than immediately blaming yourself for lacking inspiration.

sections.bodyMarkdown: The Empress and the Magician both involve creation. The Magician leans toward starting and assembling tools; the Empress asks how work can keep growing and how its environment can accommodate repeated attempts. Seen alongside the Emperor, care and structure can also support each other: regular creative time need not stifle inspiration, and suitable arrangements may protect it. Reversal asks about the effect of giving, not merely its quantity. Doing everything for someone who needs practice may look generous while actually reducing their autonomy. Adding more when you are already depleted is also unlikely to create dependable support.

sections.title: Giving a Picture-Book Draft Room to Grow
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Alu asks, “How can I keep going with this half-finished picture book?”

Known facts: She already has characters and a story, but temporary clutter takes over the table every evening and her art supplies are stored in a high cupboard. She usually waits until late at night to begin, then dislikes how rough the sketches look the next day. She draws the upright Empress in the position for support that needs adding.

Woodland, flowing water, and the soft seat direct the reading toward creative conditions. She is not entirely without ideas. What drains her is setting up again every day and feeling she must get the drawing right in one attempt. The Empress can suggest giving rough drafts room to survive: accessible materials, time that does not always fall at her most exhausted hour, and permission for a first draft to grow slowly. Abundance here means a more sustainable process, not the book's future sales.

Another possibility: If the environment is already adequate but she stopped because the plot does not work, she needs structural feedback rather than additional comfort. If she has lost interest in the story, it is worth reassessing the goal instead of forcing herself onward in the name of patient cultivation.

A practical next step: Agree with the people she lives with on a small art space she can keep set up, and reserve two periods each week when she is more alert. Draw three consecutive pages of rough storyboards without polishing them. Then ask one test reader to retell the story, checking whether the blockage lies in conditions or storytelling.

sections.title: Caring for a Friend While Returning Their Decisions
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Atong asks, “Why are we getting angry with each other more often when I'm helping organize my friend's life?”

Known facts: After her friend moved, she volunteered to choose furniture, arrange weekends, and prepare meals. Her friend thanked her but said they wanted to make decisions in their own time. Atong has already used most of her rest time. She draws the reversed Empress in the relationship-imbalance position.

The known facts support a reading of excessive care that overlooks autonomy. The Empress's water and grain can suggest provision, but real nourishment must fit the recipient's needs. The friend has explicitly asked to decide for themselves, and that statement matters more than the card. Reversal also highlights Atong's depletion: giving that depends on continually squeezing her own life can easily become entangled with expectations of a return.

Another possibility: If the friend actually requested specific help, and Atong is willing and has capacity, the problem may simply be unclear responsibilities, calling for a discussion of scope. Reversal cannot diagnose all goodwill as control, nor justify guesses about her underlying personality.

A practical next step: Stop arrangements that have not been agreed upon, ask which one kind of help the friend would like to retain, and explain how much time she can offer each week. Truly return the freed-up rest time to herself. After a week, observe whether both feel more at ease, rather than measuring the relationship by how often she is thanked.

quickTake.upright: Clear rules and responsibilities make things steadier.
quickTake.reversed: Control may be too rigid, or no one is taking responsibility where needed.

Upright in a sentence: Clear rules and responsibilities make things steadier.

Reversed in a sentence: Control may be too rigid, or no one is taking responsibility where needed.

Metal armor shows beneath the Emperor's red robe. Even seated on his throne, he has not entirely set aside his defenses. Stability can protect people and also make it hard to relax.

sections.title: Armor Remains Beneath the Red Robe
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A white-bearded elder sits facing forward on a gray stone throne, wearing a gold crown. Ram's heads decorate the two upper corners and the fronts of the armrests. title: The Hierophant: Learning a Method and Understanding Its Origins

quickTake.upright: There are established methods to learn from, and knowledgeable people to ask.
quickTake.reversed: The old way may not fit. Understand it before deciding whether to change it.

introMarkdown:

Reversed in a sentence: The old way may not fit. Understand it before deciding whether to change it.

Two listeners are gathered before the Hierophant. Knowledge here is more than one person's insight: a group receives it through ritual, roles, and a shared language.

sections.title: We Stand Behind the Listeners
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The central figure wears a red robe and triple crown, seated between two gray pillars. His hand on the left of the picture is raised in blessing; the other holds a cross-shaped staff with three crossbars. A white stole marked with crosses hangs down his chest.

In the foreground, two people kneel with their backs to us, the centers of their heads tonsured. Their garments bear rose and lily patterns respectively. Crossed keys lie between them at the Hierophant's feet. The composition separates teacher from recipients and places us behind the listeners. Compared with the partly concealed scroll held by the High Priestess, this looks more like an openly displayed form that can be transmitted.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_05_Hierophant.jpg)

Shift your gaze from crown and staff to the two listeners. For a group to receive knowledge, it usually needs shared rituals, language, and ways of recognizing it. The crossed keys may inspire the question “How does one enter?” but do not guarantee that every claim behind the door is correct. The listeners' different clothing also reminds modern readers that people learning the same method may bring different experiences. These associations come from the composition, not additional historical research into the figures' identities. If a redrawn card makes the teacher one person at a round table, the power relationship has changed and the interpretation should change with it.

sections.bodyMarkdown:

This leaves contemporary readers with two considerations: tradition can preserve experience, and it can become authority reduced to form alone. Extending this to schools, vocational training, or community norms is this article's modern application, not a claim that the original book names each of these settings.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright can encourage using a learning path that has already been tested. Consulting a teacher, joining a course with feedback, or understanding a profession's shared rules can reduce the cost of working everything out alone. You need not reinvent every step to appear independent.

When accepting guidance, you can still ask about a method's purpose, evidence, and scope. Truly learning means understanding why a rule exists and using it appropriately, rather than merely memorizing the standard answer.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Here, reversal asks whether a method fits reality. Perhaps an old process has drifted from its purpose, or you are following demands you disagree with to gain approval. Another possibility is skipping necessary foundations simply because you dislike being taught.

First clarify what you oppose: the rule itself, how it is enforced, or the person proposing it? If you want to change it, write down how the alternative will achieve the quality and fairness originally needed. Questioning and learning can happen together.

sections.bodyMarkdown: Both the Hierophant and the High Priestess encounter knowledge. The former directs attention to public teaching and organizational recognition; the latter makes room for what has not yet been said. The Hierophant also differs from the Emperor: the Emperor leans toward who implements and takes responsibility, while the Hierophant asks what counts as a collectively accepted method. Upright may mean drawing on courses and mentorship, but in an obstacle position it can suggest excessive dependence on standard answers. Reversal does not necessarily require leaving every organization. First understand what a rule is trying to protect. Then decide whether to retain the principle, modify the practice, or leave a system that no longer responds to your needs.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xiaocheng asks, “I've been learning guitar for six months. Why is playing a whole song still so difficult?”

Known facts: She has learned many fingerings through short videos, but changes songs whenever she reaches a difficult passage and has never practiced the complete rhythm slowly. At a recent open rehearsal, she found it hard to keep time with others. She draws the upright Hierophant in the helpful-learning-resources position.

The listeners before the Hierophant correspond to an opportunity to consult an established learning path. She has interest; what she lacks is continuous training and feedback that responds to mistakes. Upright may suggest finding a teacher or partner who explains the purpose of exercises and watches her actual playing, using a shared beat to connect scattered techniques. It cannot establish that a particular paid course is reliable, nor make every teacher's statement automatically true.

Another possibility: If she already has systematic training and is merely unfamiliar with a new musical style, she needs targeted rhythm practice rather than another beginner course. A course promising rapid mastery without explaining its content also warrants suspended judgment.

A practical next step: Book one trial lesson or ask an experienced partner to watch a complete performance, then identify one specific weak point. Practice the same passage slowly for a week and compare recordings for steadiness. Use practice feedback to decide whether to continue along that learning path.

sections.title: Can a Family Ritual Be Done Differently?
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Zeyu asks, “Every family meal follows the old rules. How can I suggest simplifying it?”

Known facts: The meals originally served to bring everyone together. Now one person handles almost all the preparation, while others leave early because the proceedings are elaborate. Everyone values meeting, but they have not seriously discussed which elements must stay. He draws the reversed Hierophant in the position for a custom that needs reconsidering.

This example reads reversal as form becoming detached from its original purpose. The shared ritual represented by the Hierophant really can sustain belonging, so simply saying “tradition is useless” misses the point. The actual test is whether the present practice still helps people spend time together. The preparer's burden and how long people really stay support adjustment more directly than guesses about older relatives' motives.

Another possibility: If a particular element has special commemorative meaning for someone, understand that before simplifying it rather than removing it for efficiency alone. If Zeyu simply dislikes attending, he should honestly state his own choice, not invoke a collective burden to speak for everyone.

A practical next step: Ask each person which part they most want to retain. Propose one trial gathering with shared preparation, one fewer procedural step, and time left for conversation. Afterwards, see whether people are more willing to participate before discussing a lasting change, allowing the alternative to meet the need the tradition originally carried.

title: The Lovers: From Attraction to a Shared Choice

quickTake.upright: There is mutual attraction and a willingness to choose this connection seriously.
quickTake.reversed: The feelings are there, but you are not aligned; important choices remain unspoken.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: There is mutual attraction and a willingness to choose this connection seriously.

Reversed in a sentence: The feelings are there, but you are not aligned; important choices remain unspoken.

The two people in the Lovers stand on the same grass but do not hold hands. Space remains between them, and a winged figure spreads its arms above. A relationship appears in the picture; how to move closer is still for people to work out.

sections.title: Two People Looking in Different Directions
sections.bodyMarkdown:
The sun occupies the top of the picture. A winged figure extends red wings above the clouds, palms facing outward. Below, a naked woman and man stand with their arms slightly open. The man turns toward the woman; she looks upward. A pointed mountain rises between them, and grass spreads beneath their feet.

Behind the woman is a fruit-bearing tree with a serpent coiled around its trunk. The branches of the tree behind the man take flame-like forms. We can observe different directions of looking, two different trees, and space divided into layers by cloud and mountain. Nudity may suggest honesty and vulnerability to a contemporary reader, but that is an interpretation developed from the image, not grounds for guessing the figures' inner states.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_06_Lovers.jpg)

The gap between them is useful: they share a picture without being drawn as one person. A relationship needs closeness and room for each person's expression. Their different gazes can prompt “Are we discussing the same thing?” but cannot establish who loves whom more. Mountain and winged figure place the relationship in a larger setting. A modern application can ask how outside expectations, values, and shared living affect a choice. The image provides no terms of commitment or stated relationship stage. Nudity and attraction cannot be directly converted into engagement, marriage, or inevitable intimacy.

sections.title: How Waite Reworked the Lovers' Image
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite explicitly likens the two people to Adam and Eve in Eden, mentioning the Tree of Life and Tree of Knowledge. He calls this an image of human love and rejects reducing the new picture to the older account of a man choosing between virtue and vice.

quickTake.reversed: Effort is taking you off course. Realign direction and pace first.

sections.title: Reclining Sphinxes, No Visible Reins
sections.bodyMarkdown:
An armored person stands in the chariot beneath a star-shaped crown and a blue canopy patterned with stars. Crescent ornaments with faces sit on both shoulders. A square appears on the chest, and small symbols are arranged on the fabric below the waist. The figure holds a scepter on the left of the picture, with the other hand resting at the chariot's edge.

A black and a white sphinx lie side by side before the vehicle, their heads and bodies not facing in exactly the same direction. A winged circular motif and a shield-shaped ornament decorate the chariot's center; walls, towers, and a band of water remain visible behind it. The figure's position is resolute, but the picture shows no running, spinning wheels, or dust. It should therefore not be described as charging at high speed.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_07_Chariot.jpg)

Seen together, the upright figure and reclining sphinxes suggest concentrated will without necessarily completed coordination of the conditions for movement. There are no visible reins, so leadership is not best understood solely as pulling tighter. A modern reading can begin by defining a goal, distinguishing different needs, and agreeing on a pace. The walls behind also give “leaving familiar territory” a place in the image, but no journey distance or arrival time is provided. Two colors may suggest difference without dividing forces into good and bad. In real life, speed and quality, or solitude and collaboration, may each be necessary.

sections.title: Reaching a Goal Does Not Mean Understanding Everything
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite connects the Chariot with conquest and victory, particularly achievement in intellectual and outward spheres. He also cautions that this does not mean the figure has attained inward spiritual understanding. That limit matters: winning one goal does not resolve every problem.

The original text also calls the object in the figure's hand a drawn sword, whereas the checked RWS color image visibly shows a scepter. This article describes the actual picture while retaining the textual discrepancy, rather than treating every sentence in the original book as an exact visual record.

sections.title: Understanding the Upright Card
sections.bodyMarkdown:

Motivation is already present; next come priorities, a steady pace, and keeping different needs from pulling against one another. The two sphinxes can serve as a visual cue for such coordination. Once the goal is clear, you also need the ability to adjust the route. Steady progress includes reviewing feedback, replenishing resources, and necessary rest. Persistence does not mean never turning. It means knowing why you are moving and which changes need a response.

Slow down to check, rather than invariably applying more force. Review purpose, resources, and responsibilities separately, identifying two demands that conflict. If the goal itself no longer fits, choosing a new direction is also a form of control.

It also differs from the Wheel of Fortune's external turns: the Chariot emphasizes direction you can organize, not total control of your surroundings. Even upright, check whether a “shared goal” crowds out someone's necessary boundaries.

sections.title: A Charity Sale Needs a Finish Line Everyone Recognizes
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Qinghe asks, “Our community charity sale is ten days away. How can we get preparations running smoothly?”

Known facts: Volunteers are willing to help, but the publicity team keeps expanding the event while the on-site team worries there will not be enough tables and chairs. The planning chat is busy, yet no one can clearly state the day's most important goal. Qinghe draws the upright Chariot in the approach-to-progress position.

The firmly centered figure and differently oriented sphinxes can correspond to shared willingness that has not become a shared direction. People are working hard, but their efforts pull against each other. In an advice position, the upright Chariot better suits establishing a manageable scale and basic deliverables before coordinating teams, rather than asking everyone to speed up. The card cannot predict attendance either.

Another possibility: If site permission, essential supplies, or a responsible organizer remain unconfirmed, those are real conditions that must be filled in. No clear goal can substitute for them. If the goal was already shared and the issue is missed messages, improve information flow rather than redo the entire plan.

A practical next step: Hold a short meeting solely to set the event's scope, each team's lead, and the final confirmation time. Put new ideas on a list for next time. First ensure someone is responsible for the entrance, stalls, and closing cleanup, and update only changes that genuinely affect the next step each day.

sections.title: A Trip Has a Direction, but Its Arrangements Conflict
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Anran asks, “Discussing this trip with my friend keeps getting more exhausting. Should we not travel together?”

Known facts: One person wants three sights a day; the other wants leisurely walks. Both want the trip, but they keep competing to book the next stop and have not discussed how long they can walk each day. She draws the reversed Chariot in the pace-needing-adjustment position.

Here, reversal looks more like two driving forces that have not been coordinated. The black and white sphinxes lie together without facing exactly the same way. This composition helps describe differences but cannot prove incompatibility. Fatigue comes from visible itinerary conflicts, making travel priorities the appropriate first discussion rather than escalating a short-term planning dispute into a judgment on the whole friendship.

Another possibility: If one person has clearly declined to travel together and the other keeps applying pressure, this is more than a simple pacing issue and their choice must be respected. If the main conflict comes from a changed budget, feasible arrangements need recalculation first; “meet halfway” alone will not solve it.

A practical next step: Each chooses one activity they care about most for a day, leaving other time open and allowing half a day separately. Do not add nonrefundable bookings yet. Proceed once both endorse the pace. Whether they can respect separate activities provides more useful feedback than whether they stay together every day.

title: Strength: Using Your Energy to Steady Yourself

quickTake.upright: Keep your temper and find your courage. A gentler approach can still get things done.
quickTake.reversed: Pushing harder is making things more strained. Are you forcing yourself onward or trying to overpower someone?

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Keep your temper and find your courage. A gentler approach can still get things done.

Reversed in a sentence: Pushing harder is making things more strained. Are you forcing yourself onward or trying to overpower someone?

A strong person can also soften their movements. Under pressure, this card asks how you use your strength.

sections.title: Look at Her Hands, Then the Lion's Body
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Against a broad yellow background, a woman in white bends toward an orange-red lion. She wears a floral crown, and a garland at her waist falls beside its mane. A horizontal figure-eight symbol hangs above her head. One hand rests near the lion's upper jaw and the other supports its lower jaw; neither arm is raised to strike. The lion lifts its head, mouth open and tongue visible, with its tail curling between its hind legs and all four paws still on the ground.

She wears no armor, and the image contains no weapon. Her clothes fall vertically, while the lion's body extends horizontally; stillness and movement meet at the contact of her hands. Behind them are grass, shrubs, and a blue mountain, with a fairly open view. Retain these visible relationships before naming the action. The still image alone cannot prove whether she is opening or closing the lion's mouth. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_08_Strength.jpg)

Both hands are close to the mouth; the woman is not directing the animal from far away. This close contact can suggest to modern readers that responding to a strong reaction begins with seeing clearly how it is unfolding. The garland and unarmored body also make the picture's strength something more than force meeting force. Yet this is a symbolic image, absolutely not a demonstration of how to approach a real predator. Nor can it require someone under threat to change another person through gentleness. In a life situation, locate “steadiness” in actions you can choose: pausing before a hurtful reply, for example, and then stating a boundary clearly.

sections.title: Waite's Strength Has a Religious Background
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite explicitly describes the action as closing the lion's mouth and explains that the lion has been subdued by beneficent fortitude, while the flower chain carries the symbolism of divine law. He connects one aspect of the lion with passions and specifically distinguishes his religious form of confidence from ordinary self-confidence. Reducing the card to “believe in yourself and you will succeed” loses the original context. [Waite, Part II, VIII](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar08.htm)

The discussion of emotion and action below is this site's reflective reading for contemporary life. It also does not turn the figures' genders into rules about who must be gentle or who needs taming.

sections.title: Upright: Giving Courage a Concrete Action
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright can mean that something is difficult and you can still remain clear-headed and keep doing what needs doing. Anger may alert you to a crossed boundary; fear may show that something matters. Identify the feeling before choosing a response, and strength gains a direction.

title: The Hermit: Make Room for Quiet and Look More Deeply

sections.title: The Lantern Is Held Outward, the Figure Stands Above
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Against a gray-blue background, an elderly man in a long cloak stands alone on a white mountain ridge. His hood is lowered and his white beard reaches his chest; his face turns toward the lower left of the picture. An outstretched hand raises a lantern, while the other holds a long staff. Its tip rests on the ground, forming a slender vertical line alongside his body.

A star-shaped light is visible inside the lantern, its rays extending beyond the frame. The cloak covers most of his body but does not hide the lamp. No companion, house, or clear road into the distance appears, nor does light fill the sky. The eye first catches that small patch of yellow, then moves down to the rocks at his feet. This makes “how much can be illuminated?” a very concrete observation. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_09_Hermit.jpg)

The lantern extends outside the cloak, meaning its light can be seen by others. A solitary composition need not mean rejecting every connection. The light also has a definite range; it does not turn the whole mountain landscape into daylight. A modern application can therefore hold two things together: pursue only the question most in need of understanding, and allow suitable people to offer guidance. The staff meets the ground, giving “slowing down” support rather than endless waiting in a void. The elder's appearance can suggest accumulated experience, but cannot establish that older people are always reliable or younger people have no value as guides.

title: The Wheel of Fortune: Adjusting as Circumstances Change

quickTake.upright: Things are turning. Opportunities and uncertainty arrive together; timely adjustment helps.
quickTake.reversed: Change is not keeping your pace. Steady yourself, then see which step you can alter.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Things are turning. Opportunities and uncertainty arrive together; timely adjustment helps.

Reversed in a sentence: Change is not keeping your pace. Steady yourself, then see which step you can alter.

Some changes arrive faster than a plan can accommodate. The Wheel of Fortune draws attention to timing, cycles, and the response you can still choose now.

sections.title: Follow the Wheel Around, Then Look at the Corners
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A large orange wheel occupies the center amid blue sky and clouds. Several concentric rings divide its face, with spokes extending from the center. Latin and Hebrew letters appear on the outer ring, and other symbols on an inner one. A blue sphinx sits at the top holding a sword in its forelimbs. A yellow serpent-shaped body descends on the left, while a red, long-snouted figure with a human body and animal head rises along the lower-right rim.

A winged figure occupies each corner: human at upper left, eagle at upper right, ox at lower left, lion at lower right, each with a book before it. The rim's curves and bodies at the sides suggest motion, while the corners frame the composition steadily. No one is turning a handle, and no ordinary person single-handedly controls the whole scene. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_10_Wheel_of_Fortune.jpg)

Do not rush to guess the wheel's direction: a still card does not tell us where the next turn will stop. The changing impression at the rim and steadiness of the book-bearing corner figures can help distinguish external fluctuations from practices you can maintain. The descending serpent and ascending figure also do not mean a particular real person is destined to rise or fall. Letters and symbols from different traditions require historical sources to explain them; their order cannot justify invented winning numbers. A more practical modern question is: Which conditions have changed, and which arrangements that worked before can still be kept?

sections.title: Blended Symbols Do Not Prove an Egyptian Origin
sections.bodyMarkdown: Waite says he adopted and adjusted Éliphas Lévi's conception, connects the corner figures with the four living creatures of Ezekiel, associates the wheel with life's flux, and makes the sphinx represent balance within it. He explicitly states that using Egyptian symbols does not assert an Egyptian origin for tarot. The mixed imagery belongs to this particular symbolic arrangement. [Waite, Part II, X](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar10.htm)

sections.title: Upright: Notice the Opening and Leave Some Margin
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This site reads upright as changing conditions: a previously blocked path may open, and a familiar method may need updating. You can take an opportunity while checking its time limit, participation requirements, and actual cost. Moving with circumstances means acting on new information, not treating every coincidence as an instruction.

The wheel turns, and existing progress still needs maintenance. When a collaboration has just attracted attention, organizing processes and capacity promptly is more practical than assuming the interest will last forever.

title: Justice: Put the Facts Together Before Deciding

quickTake.upright: Make the facts and criteria clear, and decide by a consistent standard.
quickTake.reversed: Judgment may be skewed. Check missing evidence, double standards, and responsibility left unclaimed.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Make the facts and criteria clear, and decide by a consistent standard.

Reversed in a sentence: Judgment may be skewed. Check missing evidence, double standards, and responsibility left unclaimed.

When something feels unfair, resist rushing to judge someone's character. Justice asks you to place evidence, standards, and each person's responsibility on the same table.

sections.title: One Hand Weighs, the Other Holds a Sword
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Justice sits facing forward between two gray pillars, eyes open and unblindfolded. A blue square adorns the gold crown. A green mantle lies over a red robe, with a purple-red veil behind. The figure's right hand, on the left of the picture, holds a long upright sword; the left holds scales, whose pans hang on the picture's right.

Body and seat are roughly centered, but the sword extends a higher vertical line while the scales spread sideways. A toe emerges from beneath the robe onto the steps. Eyes, scales, and sword together can remind the reader of “seeing clearly, weighing, acting.” This is a modern reading of the composition, not three laws written on the card. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_11_Justice.jpg)

Different hands hold scales and sword: weighing and enforcement coexist, but the step of establishing facts cannot be skipped. Her visible, open eyes also caution against importing every image of Lady Justice into this particular card; there is no blindfold here. Two pans can suggest comparison, yet real fairness does not always mean identical quantities. Include context, agreements, and degrees of control to avoid judging only the final outcome. The upright sword can suggest a clear decision, but does not demand sharp language or authorize punishing someone.

sections.title: Conduct and Corresponding Responsibility
sections.bodyMarkdown: Waite emphasizes the moral principle of giving people treatment corresponding to their actions. He also distinguishes these pillars from those beside the High Priestess, reminding readers that similar compositions need not have identical meanings. The old divinatory list does connect Justice with fairness and legal settings, but that is historical divinatory language, not a guarantee of the outcome of a present-day case. [Waite, Part II, XI](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar11.htm); [Part III, §3, entry 11](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

sections.title: Upright: Fairness Needs an Explainable Basis
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright can suit checking agreements, clarifying responsibility, and making an explainable choice. Ask: What is this decision based on? If the same thing happened to someone else, would I apply this standard?

Responsibility also includes repairing the effects of your own actions. Acknowledging an omission, completing missing work, or apologizing clearly is closer to the card's practical application than insisting “I meant well.” Fairness need not give everyone an identical amount, but the reasons for allocation should be discussable and testable.

sections.title: Reversed: Check Whether a Finger Is Pressing on the Scales
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Reversal can suggest bias, missing information, evaded responsibility, or rules that are themselves too harsh. Waite's reversed entries mention narrowness, bias, and excessive severity, providing historical parallels. This site turns that into a concrete review: Have you heard only one side, changed the criteria afterwards, or assigned one person all the consequences they could not control?

Drawing reversal proves neither that you were wrong nor that someone else was unfair. If you repeatedly blame yourself, first separate what you actually did, what can be remedied, and outcomes that were never yours to decide.

The Emperor can establish a system; Justice asks whether it can be explained to different people. Upright does not guarantee you naturally occupy the right side, and reversal does not prove you wrong. Try applying the same standard to your own account, particularly noticing whether “I meant well” excuses real impact, or “the outcome was bad” assigns you responsibility that was never yours.

sections.title: Splitting a Travel Bill Without Four Different Versions of Fairness
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Kexin asks, “Our four-person trip is over. How should we split shared expenses fairly?”

Known facts: One person left a day early, and another advanced transport costs for everyone. The group assumed an equal split without confirming whether that included personal purchases and different numbers of nights. All receipts remain available. Kexin draws upright Justice in the guiding-principle position.

The scales correspond to comparing like categories; the sword reminds them to reach a clear decision after checking. The known issue is that chargeable scope and allocation criteria were not clarified. Showing records first and then discussing the basis for shared costs is appropriate. “Upright Justice” cannot declare one person's calculation inherently fair, and the loudest voice cannot substitute for collective confirmation.

Another possibility: If they explicitly agreed before departure to split everything equally, first check that agreement, then discuss whether all agree to an adjustment. If receipts are missing, mark estimates rather than inventing numbers to settle quickly.

A practical next step: List each item, payer, actual users, and any agreed allocation, removing personal spending from the shared bill. Give everyone one chance to check, then set deadlines for payment and additional claims. Discuss disputed items separately so unconfirmed entries do not hold up the whole settlement.

sections.title: A Group Project Scored Poorly: Is It All My Fault?
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Qiuyuan asks, “Our group presentation went badly. Did I let everyone down?”

Known facts: He was responsible for illustrations and delivered half a day late, but the presentation also had unverified information and missed rehearsals. Someone in the group attributes the entire low score to his delay, and he keeps blaming himself. He draws reversed Justice in the judgment-needing-correction position.

Reversal can suggest distorted allocation of responsibility. The scales invite separating each action and its actual effect. The late delivery does deserve ownership, but cannot automatically explain every problem. Rather than first assume the critic is malicious, check the evidence linking causes and outcomes. Qiuyuan should also avoid using “everyone made mistakes” to erase the inconvenience his delay caused.

Another possibility: If the teacher's feedback explicitly says missing pictures directly caused the absence of a central part of the presentation, his share of responsibility may be greater. If the pictures were supplied in time and did not affect the presentation, reassess. Read feedback and time records instead of dividing blame evenly according to feelings.

A practical next step: Clearly acknowledge and remedy his own late delivery first, then invite the group to review how each task affected the presentation. Write down delivery and rehearsal milestones for next time. Evaluate specific behavior and improvements without labeling anyone “always the one who drags us down.”

title: The Hanged Man: Pause and Look from Another Angle

quickTake.upright: Pause, change your perspective, and clarify what is worth giving.
quickTake.reversed: You have been stuck a long time. Are you waiting for conditions, or spending time without being willing to change?

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Pause, change your perspective, and clarify what is worth giving.

Reversed in a sentence: You have been stuck a long time. Are you waiting for conditions, or spending time without being willing to change?

The more urgently you struggle free, the more you may repeat the same movement. The Hanged Man turns the question upside down, allowing a pause to become part of observation.

sections.title: The Body Is Inverted, but the Tree Still Has Leaves
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A leafy crossbeam and an upright trunk form an approximately T-shaped frame. One ankle is fastened to the beam, leaving the figure suspended head downward. The other leg bends behind the straight leg. A blue tunic, red trousers, and pale shoes divide the body into clear areas. Both arms bend behind the back, and the hands are not visible.

A circle of yellow radiance surrounds the head, with no exaggerated expression of pain on the face. The background is almost blank, with neither spectators nor an ongoing struggle. Leaves, light, and the suspended body create a particular tension together: outward action has stopped, but the picture does not show complete exhaustion of life. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_12_Hanged_Man.jpg)

The body is inverted while the trunk stays upright. What has changed is the observer's relationship to the environment, not the whole world's orientation. This can inspire a specific exercise: change “How do I persuade them?” to “Why is this hard for them to accept?” and see what you previously missed. Halo and leaves give the pause a living quality, but the picture does not state how long the suspension lasts or how the figure arrived. It therefore cannot guarantee a reward for waiting. An upright pause needs an observable question; reversed stagnation calls for checking whether understanding has increased, rather than counting only the time already given.

sections.title: Do Not Overlook Waite's Emphasis on Life
sections.bodyMarkdown: Waite asks readers to notice three things: the wooden frame is living, the face expresses absorption rather than suffering, and the whole figure suggests life in suspension. He places the card in a context of mystical awakening and resurrection and rejects its simple classification as martyrdom. Directly concluding “you must sacrifice yourself” is not faithful to his explanation. [Waite, Part II, XII](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar12.htm)

sections.title: Upright: Bring a Question into the Pause
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This site's modern reading is to put a habitual method aside temporarily and notice what the speed of action had obscured. Postponing, waiting, or leaving an argument can create space to observe. The key is knowing what you stopped to look at.

Trade-offs are another layer. You might willingly do less for a while or surrender a convenience in exchange for learning or clearer judgment. The cost should be specific, manageable, and your choice. The image does not tell us how the figure arrived, still less authorize deciding for a real person that “they suffer willingly.”

sections.title: Reversed: Does This Wait Still Serve a Purpose?
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Reversal can ask whether the pause has produced new information. Repeatedly moving deadlines without anyone responsible for the next step may simply be stagnation. Conversely, rushing to resume before conditions are ready can bring the original problem back unchanged.

Waite's old list connects upright with discernment, trial, and sacrifice, but gives reversal asymmetrical terms including selfishness and the crowd; it does not directly say “procrastination.” This article's checks on waiting limits and boundaries are practical exercises developed by this site. [Waite, Part III, §3, entry 12](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

sections.title: Distinguishing Related Meanings
sections.bodyMarkdown: The Hanged Man and Hermit can both slow action, but the Hanged Man emphasizes loosening an existing posture or habitual method, while the Hermit leans toward focused inquiry. title: Death: Bringing What Has Ended to a Real Close

quickTake.upright: This phase needs to end. Put the old things in order and make room for what follows.
quickTake.reversed: You know change is needed but still hesitate to let go. Find one old thing you can release.

introMarkdown:

Reversed in a sentence: You know change is needed but still hesitate to let go. Find one old thing you can release.

sections.title: The Rider Has No Scythe, but the Flag Has a Flower
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A skeleton in black armor rides a white horse toward the right. It raises a black flag bearing a white five-petaled flower; no sword or scythe is visible in its hand. The white horse fills the center, one foreleg raised, leading the eye toward the people ahead.

At lower left, someone lies on the ground with a gold crown nearby. On the right, a person in a tall headdress and gold ceremonial robe faces the rider with hands together. Lower down are a kneeling child and a young person with face turned aside. A small boat appears on the water behind, and a radiant sun emerges between two distant towers. Black-and-white flag, people of different status, and distant light share the picture, making both “ending” and “continuing” visible. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_13_Death.jpg)

People of different statuses appear before the rider, suggesting to modern readers that a phase's ending is not determined only by personal position or wishes. This is not a definite account of every pictured person's fate, much less a basis for calculating lifespan. The distant sun provides a symbolic direction of “a world remains after change” without canceling the weight of loss nearby. The horse's forward movement and the fallen person create a sense of time, helping us ask what has already happened and what unfinished closing work still waits. Keep the flower, flag, and distant landscape in view rather than reducing everything to a frightening card name.

sections.title: Renewal's Symbolism Retains the Weight of Ending
sections.bodyMarkdown:

[Waite, Part II, XIII](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar13.htm)

This article adopts a symbolic reading of everyday life. Drawing this card cannot predict anyone's death, illness, or lifespan. It better helps with an ending that has already happened or has genuine signs in reality.

sections.title: Upright: Closing Is Work Too
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright can mean acknowledging that an old form can no longer continue: a project ends, an identity changes, or a habit loses its use. Specific farewell tasks often follow, such as returning belongings, completing a handover, organizing records, or allowing yourself time to adjust.

A new stage need not feel immediately exciting. You can know change is necessary and still miss the people and things that came before. Acknowledging that complexity is more honest than forcing instant positivity. The card cannot prove a relationship must end; major decisions still require real facts.

sections.title: Reversed: Loosen One Small Thing at the Old Doorway
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Reversal can examine an unfinished goodbye: saying something is over while repeatedly reopening it in action, or continually postponing all sorting to avoid sadness. Waite's reversed list includes inertia and rigidity, providing a historical clue for “standing still.” This article extends it into reflection on delayed closure and fear of change. Adjustment may also simply need time. Do not turn “not yet letting go” into another accusation. First distinguish responsibilities that must be handled from emotions that can unfold gradually.

Mixing the two can make people think putting belongings away requires instantly ceasing to feel sad.

sections.title: Saying a Proper Goodbye After a Club Closes
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Lingyu asks, “Our weekend film group has decided to close after many years. How should I bring it to an end?”

Known facts: The venue is no longer available, and the main organizers have confirmed they cannot continue. Members know this, but borrowed equipment, photographs, and unpaid venue costs remain scattered among several people. Lingyu draws upright Death in the next-step position.

The ending here is supported by a real decision, not announced by the Death card. The rider's continued movement and distant light can direct attention to people and matters still needing care after the farewell. Upright allows sadness while reminding Lingyu that closing is concrete work: ending the activity and erasing shared experience are different things.

Another possibility: If other members genuinely want to take over and have a venue, the organizational form might change rather than stop entirely. That needs definite new commitments. Regret alone cannot keep pressing old responsibilities onto people who have stepped away.

A practical next step: List returns, payments, and notifications, confirming who will complete each. With the relevant people's consent, organize public activity records worth keeping. Arrange a brief goodbye and state the experience they want to retain, without promising a restart date for which no one has taken responsibility.

sections.title: The Old Studio Is Gone, but the Boxes Stay Closed
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xiaorui asks, “Since moving my creative work home, why have I kept avoiding sorting things from my old studio?”

Known facts: She moved out when the lease ended, and her new creative corner is usable. Old boxes mix borrowed tools needing return with her sketches. She occasionally opens a little, then worries that finishing the sorting would somehow deny that period of her life. She draws reversed Death in the difficulty-with-turning-toward-the-next-stage position.

Reversal can correspond to a goodbye still at the threshold. The facts show that the space has ended while emotions have not caught up. That does not make her lazy or oblige her to recover quickly. The flower on the flag and distant landscape can help her understand that keeping meaningful parts and acknowledging the old form's end can coexist. Returning tools comes first; deciding which sketches to keep can take time.

Another possibility: If the main reason the boxes cannot be sorted is a lack of storage in the new space, address placement first instead of explaining everything as reluctance to let go. If they contain material tied to painful private experiences, a trusted person can accompany her and the amount handled at once can be reduced.

A practical next step: Today, separate only other people's belongings and arrange their return, then choose one sketch that best represents that time to preserve carefully. Sort the remaining materials in batches at an adjustable pace. Observe whether the freed space supports one new creative session.

title: Temperance: Adjusting the Mix So Different Needs Can Work Together

quickTake.upright: Don't use all your energy in one burst. Adjust proportions and pace to help things run more smoothly.
quickTake.reversed: The mix or rhythm is off. First find what there is too much of, and what is missing.

introMarkdown:
Upright in a sentence: Don't use all your energy in one burst. Adjust proportions and pace to help things run more smoothly.

Reversed in a sentence: The mix or rhythm is off. First find what there is too much of, and what is missing.

Water is still flowing between the two cups. Temperance concerns ongoing adjustment: how to combine time, energy, and needs so something can last.

sections.title: Adjusting Water by Hand, Standing in Two Places
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A white-robed angel spreads red wings, eyes lowered toward two gold cups held at different heights. A diagonal blue stream connects them. A dot-in-circle symbol appears on the forehead with rays around it. On the chest, an upward triangle sits inside a square, with lettering visible above.

One foot stands in water, the other on the bank, rather than the feet being together. Yellow flowers and long green leaves grow on the right. On the left, a path winds through green rises toward blue mountains, with yellow radiance beyond. The figure is steady, yet neither cups nor feet are arranged in perfect symmetry. Maintaining this posture needs continuing coordination. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_14_Temperance.jpg)

The cups do not simply each hold half the water, nor are water and land mixed into one beneath the feet. The picture can remind us that cooperation may preserve difference, and harmonizing remains a process. Following the narrow stream to the distant path shows that small present adjustments and a longer direction can coexist. A modern application might change one proportion and observe the result rather than reorganizing an entire life at once. The stream's direction belongs to a symbolic image; it requires no invented physical mechanism. Symbols on forehead and chest also cannot reveal a personal medication dose or bodily measurement.

sections.title: Harmonizing Is an Active Process
sections.bodyMarkdown: Waite calls the flow between the cups a pouring of the essences of life, and explains that although he uses a masculine pronoun, the angel is neither male nor female. He places the feet on land and water, distant light, and crown within religious symbolism of life, ending with the harmonizing of spiritual and material natures. The distant crown is unclear in the scan, so it is presented here as Waite's interpretation rather than something everyone can immediately see. [Waite, Part II, XIV](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar14.htm)

sections.title: Upright: Adjust Gradually Toward Something Sustainable
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This site uses Temperance to discuss proportion and coordination. You do not need to do the maximum every time. Observe what a little more or less changes, then find a mix suited to current conditions. Study and rest, speaking and listening, planning and flexibility may all need this back-and-forth adjustment.

Two coexisting needs do not mean an equal half is automatically fair. Sometimes the more urgent side must be handled first, then recovery arranged for the other. What matters is continuing to see the whole, rather than treating one number as a permanently correct standard.

sections.title: Reversed: Locate the Actual Mismatch
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Reversal can suggest unbalanced investment, incompatible ways of collaborating, or too many changes scattering the rhythm. Ask which two parts fail to connect: conflicting schedules, missing handover information, or constant swings between rushing and complete stoppage?

Waite's upright list includes moderation and management; reversal includes disunion and competing interests, alongside older associations such as religious institutions. This article uses the former as reading cues without reducing the whole card to a health diagnosis. Temperance cannot decide medication doses, dietary restrictions, or treatment plans for you. [Waite, Part III, §3, entry 14](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

sections.title: Distinguishing Related Meanings
sections.bodyMarkdown: Temperance and Justice are both easily summarized as balance. Justice looks more at whether standards and responsibilities are reasonable; Temperance asks how different parts connect in operation. Compared with Strength, Temperance need not involve steadying a reaction in an intense moment. It may be the repeated adjustment of time across an ordinary week. In reversal, break “everything has been chaotic” into specific conflicts: starting too late, too little handover information, or changing too much at once? Alter only one observable condition at a time to identify what genuinely helps. When a request crosses a threshold of safety or respect, refusal is more appropriate than compromise.

sections.title: Learning a Language Together Without Sharing One Speed

**Original fictional case.** Qingqing asks, “My friend and I meet to practice conversation. How can we keep it up?”

Known facts: She wants to correct pronunciation slowly, while her friend wants more discussion of content. Every session becomes an argument between correction and free conversation. Both still want to continue and have a regular half hour each week. She draws upright Temperance in the collaboration-advice position.

The movement between two cups can inspire a process linking different goals, while feet on land and water acknowledge both needs. The problem has a clear scope: not whose learning style is more correct, but how thirty minutes can accommodate accuracy and fluency. Upright Temperance suits designing an adjustable proportion without requiring both interests to become the same goal.

Another possibility: If her friend does not actually want to continue and is simply embarrassed to refuse, dividing time will not solve willingness. If their levels differ too greatly, they may need more suitable practice partners; “accommodate each other” cannot bear every difference.

After two weeks, each names one helpful and one uncomfortable aspect. sections.title: Swinging Between Constant Replies and Total Disconnection
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Jiamu asks, “I'm either answering messages nonstop or turning them off and forgetting to check all day. How can I adjust?”

Known facts: He works on an amateur theater production, needing both to respond to rehearsal changes and to reserve uninterrupted time for scenery drawings. All messages currently use the same alert, mixing ordinary chat with same-day changes. He draws reversed Temperance in the source-of-imbalance position.

Reversal fits two needs without an appropriate connection. The narrow stream between higher and lower cups suggests rhythmic information exchange, rather than simply “look at your phone less.” Messages he must answer genuinely affect others, and focus time genuinely matters. Treating everything as equally urgent causes the alternation between all-on and all-off.

Another possibility: If the theater group demands constant availability without a reasonable response window, renegotiation is needed rather than further personal optimization to accommodate unlimited demands. If message volume is actually low, he may simply have failed to set clear checking times.

A practical next step: Distinguish same-day changes from ordinary discussion with the team and agree on a contact method for urgent matters. Schedule several regular checking windows each day, concentrating on drawings in between. After a week, check whether important information was missed and adjust frequency, rather than aiming never to be interrupted.
